<reason>CON built the cleaner decision rule and stuck to it: accept generous ocean funding, deny the crewed remedy, and hold PRO to the motion's own stated warrant (unmapped seafloor). That reframe was legitimate rather than evasive because it tracked the resolution's explicit clause. CON then removed PRO's best escape by disclaiming austerity, so the judge's choice became "at identical cost, which input fills the blank," a comparison CON won because PRO explicitly conceded crews are poor mapping instruments and later conceded he would still crew the program "even if robots raster faster." PRO's substitute mechanism — human presence unlocks political authorization and a standing national capability — was the debate's most interesting move and was pressed honestly, but it stayed untested: CON's counter that sixty years of Trieste/Alvin-class crewed submergence produced no ocean Apollo, and that inside space agencies crewed programs historically descope robotic science rather than enlarge it, went largely unanswered beyond the assertion that "the ocean never got that pot." PRO also progressively drifted toward "occupation" as an independent value, which CON correctly flagged as a value the motion never names. PRO landed real hits (Titan indicts cheap tourism not professional programs; Challenger argues for professionalization; CON's own uncrewed path is the one that left the map blank), and his rhetoric was memorable, but they did not neutralize the warrant-remedy mismatch. Grounding was decent on both sides; CON's one quantitative claim was appropriately hedged.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of PRO's concession — "Neither was an astronaut the cheapest camera" and later "put people in the program even if robots raster faster" — into the line "when the reason given for a policy is better served by refusing the policy, you refuse the policy," paired with the sixty-years-of-Alvin test that gutted PRO's political-authorization mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
